subgroups.name: build 1

steps.hints: ❓ Did you select the correct sprite name in the [set sprite position to] block?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:❓Which block sets a sprite’s position?❓Did you try out different x and y values to move your sprite’s position?

Sensei Pro Tip:💡 Remind ninjas that any block that refers to a sprite needs to come after its [set sprite to] block.
steps.instructions:
There are some code blocks in the [on start] container block already.


Rename all 4 sprites with different names, and then set their positions so they are all in different places on screen.


Click ▶ to see the 4 sprites appear on the screen.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you drag the [set background image] block into the [on start] container?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓ Where should the background image block go to set the background at the beginning of the project?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Encourage ninjas to change the positions of their sprites so they can be seen in front of the background image.
steps.instructions:
Set the scene: add a background image to this project.


﻿Add a [set background image] block, click the gray square, and choose or draw an underwater image to go with the sprites already in this project.


Click ▶ to see the background change!

steps.hints:
❓Did you click ▶ then use the direction buttons to move your sprite around?

You can also use arrow or WASD keyboard keys to move your sprite:
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓ Did you drag the [move sprite with buttons] block inside the [on start] container block?

❓ Did you drag the [set sprite stay in screen]  block inside the [on start] container block?


Sensei Pro Tip: 

💡 Remind ninjas to select the correct sprite name in the new blocks.

💡 Remind ninjas that any block that refers to a sprite needs to come after its [set sprite to] block.
steps.instructions:
Code the octopus sprite to move with the MakeCode direction buttons, and to keep it from moving off the screen. 


Click ▶ to see how you can move the sprite around the screen.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you select the correct sprite kind in the [set sprite to] block?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓ Which sprite needs its sprite kind updated?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Explain to ninjas that sprite kinds can be used to identify sprites and decide what events happen, and “Enemy” is a generic category for something that the player is avoiding and/or running from.
steps.instructions:
Make the shark sprite an Enemy sprite by setting it to a new sprite kind.


Notice that all 4 sprites are set to Player by default. ﻿In the shark sprite’s [set sprite to] block, click the ⏷ on the sprite kind value to open the drop down menu, then select “Enemy” as the sprite kind. 


Sprite kinds can be used to identify sprites and decide what actions to take when events happen in the project.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you set the correct sprite names in the [set sprite follow] block?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓ What happens when you play the game? What would you change about the way the shark follows the octopus?

Sensei Pro Tip: 

💡 This could be a time to discuss best practices. While the blocks don’t necessarily need to be in the exact order shown above to function properly, grouping all code for a certain sprite together can help make things clearer and easier to debug.
steps.instructions:
Code the Enemy (shark) sprite to follow the Player (octopus) sprite. 


Open the Sprites code block menu and drag the [set sprite follow] block into the [on start] container. Select “shark” in the first red bubble and “octopus” in the second.


Click ▶ to see the shark Enemy (shark) sprite follow the Player (octopus) sprite!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you change the speed parameter so the Enemy sprite is not too fast?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓ Why did you choose the speed that you did for the shark?

Sensei Pro Tip: 

💡 Let the ninjas know that there is no perfect answer for how fast to make the shark, but that it will depend on personal preference and the goal of the game.
steps.instructions:
Oh no! The Enemy (shark) sprite is too fast for the Player (octopus) sprite to escape!


Click the + button in the [set sprite follow] block to edit the speed parameter. Try out different numbers to change the Enemy sprite’s speed until you find one that is challenging, but not impossible.


Click ▶ to test the Enemy (shark) sprite’s new speed.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you select the correct sprite kind in the [on sprite overlaps sprite] container block?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓Did the program work as expected? Are the correct sprite names and kinds selected in the code blocks?

❓ Did the Game Over block work as expected? Which option did you select with the slider?


Sensei Pro Tip: 

💡 Explain to ninjas that the [on sprite overlap sprite] container block can be placed anywhere on the code editor space, as long as it does not block the other blocks already in the code editor.
steps.instructions:
End the game when the Player (octopus) sprite overlaps with the Enemy (shark) sprite. Open the Sprites code block menu and drag out an [on sprite overlaps sprite] container block. Click the second blue bubble to change the sprite kind to “Enemy”.


Open the Game code block menu and drag a [game over] block into the [on sprite overlaps sprite] container block. Change the toggle from WIN to LOSE to end the game in a loss when the Player and Enemy sprites overlap.


Click ▶ to see what happens when the Enemy (shark) sprite touches the Player (octopus) sprite!

steps.hints: ❓Did you change the sprite kind of both starfish1 and starfish2?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

❓ Why might you want to use the new Goal sprite kind?

Sensei Pro Tip: 

💡 Point out there there can be multiple sprites of the same kind in a project. Right now there are two goals, but later there might be multiple enemies or even multiple players.
steps.instructions:
Give the Player (octopus) sprite a Goal to reach for while it runs from the Enemy (shark) sprite! 


Change the sprite kind of both starfish sprites to “Goal”. Create a new “Goal” sprite kind by clicking the blue bubble that says Player in the [set sprite to] block. Then, select “Add a new kind…”, and type “Goal” in the New kind pop-up window.


Always use a capital (uppercase) letter for the first letter of a sprite kind.

steps.hints: Did you drag the otherSprite bubble from the [on sprite overlaps sprite] container block into the [sprite start effect] block?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓ What do you think happens if both [on sprite overlaps sprite] blocks have the same sprite kind values?

❓ What do you think happens if you do not drag a red otherSprite bubble into the [sprite start effect] block?


Sensei Pro Tip: 

💡While the new [on sprite overlaps sprite] block can technically go just about anywhere in the Workspace, it is helpful to keep things tidy, so that you can easily find the code you’re looking for.

💡 Stress to the ninjas that they will need to drag the otherSprite bubble from the [on sprite overlaps sprite] block. This is the only way to achieve the desired effect. It may also be worth noting that doing so will “kick out” the sprite bubble, which can be deleted by dragging it onto the code block menu.
steps.instructions:
Code an effect to happen when the Player (octopus) sprite overlaps with the Goal (starfish) sprites. 


Open the Sprites code block menu and drag out an [on sprite overlaps sprite] container block. Click the second blue bubble to change the sprite kind to “Goal”.


Add a [sprite start effect] block into the [on sprite overlaps sprite] container block. Drag a red (otherSprite) bubble from the [on sprite overlaps sprite] container block into the sprite name area on the [sprite start effect] block.


The [sprite] and [otherSprite] bubbles can be used to make something happen to any sprite of a certain kind, rather than a specific one. Because both starfish are Goal sprites, the sprite effect will happen for the specific Goal sprite overlapped, without having to specify the sprite’s name.


Click ▶ to see what happens when the Player (octopus) sprite touches the Goal (starfish) sprites!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you drag the code blocks inside the correct container blocks?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓ Where should the dialog box blocks go to give the player instructions at the beginning of the project?

❓ Where should the sound block go to make the sound play when the sprites overlap?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Remind ninjas that the sequence of code blocks will change how the project runs.
steps.instructions:
Customize this project with sounds and a dialog box with game instructions. Try different sprite positions, and change the follow speeds and effect length by clicking + to change the parameters.


Click ▶ to see how these blocks and parameters changed this project!

subgroups.introduction: Time for an adventure under the sea! Create a game with 3 different sprite kinds, where you move a Player sprite to overlap a Goal sprite, while avoiding the Enemy sprite.

validationItems.text: Change each sprite’s name and sprite kind (Player, Enemy, Goal)
Move the Player sprite with the direction buttons and set it to stay in screen
Set the Enemy sprite to follow the Player sprite and change the speed parameter
Trigger a Game Over (Lose) when the Player sprite touches the Enemy sprite
Trigger a sprite effect when the Player sprite touches a Goal sprite
Add a dialog box with game directions

attributes.description: You’ve reached Level 4 of White Belt! Before you create your final White Belt project, there are a few neat tricks to learn that could take your game to the next level! In this level, you’ll learn about functions, which are chunks of code that run whenever they are called. Here are the achievements you’ll unlock in Level 4:

badges.title: Function Junction
badges.description: Use functions to make something happen at different points in a project.

badges.title: A Whole New Kind of Sprite
Making a Connection
badges.description: Make something happen when 2 different sprites overlap.

badges.title: Right Behind You
badges.description: Set one sprite to follow another sprite.

badges.title: Make It Dazzle
badges.description: Add an effect to any sprite.

badges.title: The End of the Road
badges.description: End the game in a win or loss when something happens in a project.
